qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture one. Reliable, scalable and maintainable systems. This is what keeps a data system working.
One big server does the work, up to six thousand requests a second.
One big server does all the work.
At nine thousand, it drops the extra three thousand.
Too many requests get dropped.
Then it crashes. Every request is turned away.
One crash, and everything is down.
Even a planned repair takes it offline.
Even a repair means downtime.
So we keep a copy in London and in New York.
Against crashes, keep a copy in each city.
Then the link between them is cut.
Now the link is cut.
London sells a ticket and says four. New York never hears, and still says five.
London sells a ticket; New York never hears.
A customer asks New York. If it stays consistent, it refuses to answer.
Stay consistent: refuse to answer.
If it stays available, it answers five, which is stale.
Stay available: answer, maybe stale.
A database stores data today, so it is still there tomorrow.
A database stores data for tomorrow.
A cache keeps a copy of the answer close by.
A cache keeps answers close.
A hit takes two milliseconds. A miss goes to the database and takes a hundred.
A hit takes 2 ms, a miss 100 ms.
An index needs about twenty checks, instead of a million.
An index: 20 checks, not a million.
A batch job crunches the day's data overnight.
A batch job crunches it overnight.
Take ten thousand disks. About one dies every day.
10,000 disks: about one dies every day.
Over a week, seven die. Each dead disk is a fault.
A dead disk is a fault.
With one copy, a dead disk means no answer. That is a failure.
One copy: a dead disk is a failure.
With two copies, the other disk answers, and users notice nothing.
Two copies: users notice nothing.
Faults will happen. They must not become failures.
Faults must not become failures.
Six servers share a load of four hundred and twenty, seventy each.
Six servers share the load, 70 each.
One dies. The other five carry eighty-four each, and the service survives.
One dies; five carry on at 84 each.
Another dies. Now it is one hundred and five each, over the limit of one hundred.
One more dies: 105 each, over 100.
Overloaded servers fall one by one, and the load on the rest keeps growing.
Overload makes them fall one by one.
The last one cannot carry all four hundred and twenty.
The last one carries all 420.
A software bug is different. It hits all six servers at once.
One bug hits all six together.
A hundred requests, each timed, fall into bins by response time.
100 requests, each timed.
Most are quick. A few are slow, which makes a long tail.
Most are quick; a few are slow.
The blue line is the average, two hundred and fifty milliseconds.
The average is 250 ms.
The orange line is p ninety-five. Ninety-five in a hundred are faster.
p95: 95 in 100 are faster.
The red line is p ninety-nine. Ninety-nine in a hundred are faster.
p99: 99 in 100 are faster.
The slowest took over eight hundred milliseconds, and the average never shows it.
The average hides the slowest.
Cat writes a post. In the first approach, it is stored once.
Approach 1: one write per post.
When Ana reads, it takes three lookups and a merge.
Reading means 3 lookups and a merge.
In the second approach, the post is copied to each follower. Cat has five.
Approach 2: copy to each follower.
Now Ana's timeline is ready in her mailbox. Reading is one lookup.
Reading is one lookup.
Reads are far more common than posts, about sixty-five to one.
Reads outnumber posts 65 to 1.
So we copy on write. Four thousand six hundred posts, times seventy-five followers, is three hundred and forty-five thousand writes a second.
So fan out: 345,000 writes a second.
A celebrity with thirty million followers needs eighty-seven seconds. The goal is five.
A celebrity post takes 87 s, not 5.
So it is a hybrid. Celebrities are merged when you read.
Hybrid: celebrities merge on read.
Suppose we need eight times the capacity of one machine.
Need 8 times the capacity of one machine.
The big machine costs about four times more, thirty-four thousand pounds against eight thousand eight hundred.
One big machine costs about 4 times more.
If one dies, the big machine leaves nothing. The grid keeps eighty-eight per cent.
One dies: nothing left, or 88% left.
At forty times, no single machine is big enough. Only the grid can grow.
Only scale out reaches 40x, but must coordinate.
A maintainable system is easy to run, to understand, and to change.
Easy to run, understand and change.
Five services each use four databases. That is twenty connections.
Every service uses every database.
To replace one database, all five services must be edited.
Swap a database: edit all five.
A layer in between makes it nine connections.
A layer in between: 9 connections.
Now only the layer changes.
Now only the layer changes.
A fault is not a failure, if there is spare capacity.
When the load grows, add machines to share it.
Keep systems easy to run, to understand and to change.
